A (very) surface-level history of agentic AI 1966 Eliza, The first chatbot, ever. Created by Joseph Weizenbaum to simulate a psychotherapist, using simple pattern matching and substitution methodology. Worked by pairing words that patients entered into a computer with a list of pre-scripted responses. 1995 A.L.I.C.E Artificial Linguistic Internet Computer Entity (A.L.I.C.E) is a chatbot that used heuristic pattern matching to have conversations. Invented by Richard Wallace in 1995, it relied on an XML schema known as artificial intelligence markup language (AIML), which specifies conversation rules. The program simulates chatting with a real person over the Internet – in this case, Alice, a young woman who can divulge personal details and answer easy questions. 2001 Smarterchild 90’s kids can’t forget SmarterChild. At one point, it amassed 10 million users and was getting a billion messages a day. This temperamental chatbot was baked into AOL Instant Messenger (AIM) and MSN Messenger with the power to carry out fun conversations, with some additional data access to popular services at the time, like the weather and Moviefone. It’s widely considered a successful show of “conversational computing”. 2010-2014 Digital Assistants With the explosion of the iPhone came Siri for Apple iOS in 2010–an intelligent assistant and navigator that uses a natural language interface built on machine learning. Google followed suit with Google Assistant, originally launched in 2012 under a different name. Then came Cortana and Alexa in 2014. All of these digital assistants brought interactive voice into the mix, helping users send emails and texts, play music, place calls and find files, locations, and general information. 2018-2026 Large Language Models We’ll get to ChatGPT in a second. Large language models – neural networks with tons (billions) of parameters, trained on large quantities of text – came about in 2018. BERT was first on scene with 340 million parameters. But OpenAI wasn’t far behind, and shocked the world with GPT-3 in 2020, an LLM that boasted 175 billion parameters. After some fine-tuning, a variant called GPT-3.5 was made available to the public in 2022 in the form of a web interface. You guessed it. ChatGPT, the fastest growing app in history, generates human-like text and can carry out a variety of tasks, including writing scripts and translating books. Today Hyro is part of a rich history of conversational innovation and agentic AI. The model spoke fluently and offered slots that didn’t exist, times that were never really on the calendar. We tried again as the models improved, and for a long stretch it still wasn’t reliable enough to put in front of a patient. Getting it right took three years and several generations of these models, and why we waited that long is the whole story of how we built it. Scaling agentic AI means changing the workflow Share this post Key takeaways: Scaling agentic AI requires unified governance across IT, clinical, operational, legal, and executive teams. Trust is built through smaller, lower-risk workflows before AI agents move into higher-stakes use cases. AI agents expose inconsistent workflows, making standardization and change management critical to scaling. Many health systems are already beyond the pilot stage with agentic AI. They’ve tested use cases, proven the technology can work, and are now trying to scale it across more workflows, teams, and care settings. That shift is happening quickly. Hyro’s 2026 Healthcare AI Agent Benchmark Report found that 94% of current users consider AI agents critical to their 2026 operations. But the processes around those deployments are still catching up: only 59% use standardized frameworks to measure performance, while 40% still rely on informal approaches. That’s where a different set of problems starts to surface: governance teams have to coordinate more stakeholders, leaders have to build trust workflow by workflow, and operational teams have to standardize processes before AI agents can scale. At a recent CHIME Innovation Summit roundtable, digital health leaders from health systems already implementing agentic AI compared notes on what happens after the pilot. Across very different organizations, the same issues kept surfacing: overlapping governance, uneven trust, and workflows that were never standardized enough to scale. In complex care environments, health systems may need to coordinate not only their own agentic AI policies but those of partner organizations and technology vendors. In other words, the challenge of scaling agentic AI is no longer just technical. It depends on whether the organization can align governance, build trust, and standardize the workflows AI agents are expected to run. The conversation to start today Share this post Key takeaways The best time to plan an agentic AI investment is before your budget opens, not after. Work backward from your budget date to determine when evaluation, procurement, legal review, and internal approvals need to begin. Missing the formal budget window doesn’t always mean waiting another year, but it does mean exploring a different funding path. If you’re evaluating agentic AI for patient access, the operational need is probably already clear. The next challenge is making sure the evaluation, procurement, and budgeting timelines all line up. Before you schedule another demo, find out when your budget opens. Then ask one more question: when does finance need the business case? Those two dates determine when your evaluation really needs to begin. This is where many promising initiatives lose a year. The team begins evaluating solutions, narrows the field, and only then asks when the budget request is due. By that point, legal may still be reviewing terms, procurement may not have begun, and finance may already be finalizing next year’s priorities. The problem wasn’t a lack of budget. The project wasn’t ready when funding decisions were made. One way to avoid that is by treating the budget date as the fixed point and planning backward from there. Once you know what must be ready, and by when, the evaluation timeline becomes much easier to manage. Start with the budget date, not the vendor shortlist Every health system has a budget calendar. The difference is whether you build your evaluation around it or discover its importance too late. According to the Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA), fiscal year-end dates vary across hospitals , with government-sponsored organizations commonly operating on different schedules than private health systems. Some health systems plan around the calendar year. Others, particularly state- and government-affiliated organizations, follow different fiscal calendars and frequently begin their fiscal year on October 1st, mirroring the federal government’s October 1–September 30 fiscal calendar . Whatever your organization’s cycle, it should define your evaluation timeline from the very beginning, not after you’ve narrowed the vendor list or started procurement.
